query: Many physical and chemical fabrication approaches have produced multi-element, near-equiatomic solid-solution nanoparticles, yet their synthesis–structure–property relationships remain poorly established. This limits evaluation of their suitability for catalytic operation at 773–1173 K and thermoelectric use at 473–1923 K, including catalytic settings where low noble-metal content is desirable. What governs whether these nanoparticles preserve structural and chemical stability under such service regimes, and why? Formulate one testable mechanistic hypothesis, specify a controlled intervention that separates it from competing explanations, predict observations relative to a baseline, define its boundary conditions, connect it to the prior evidence summarized above, and provide a clear falsification test.

generation.hypothesis: In high‐temperature service conditions, multi‐element, near‐equiatomic solid-solution nanoparticles that have minimized lattice strain from atomic radius mismatches will resist diffusion-driven elemental segregation and surface oxidation better than those with larger mismatches.
generation.material_initial_state: Multi-element, near‐equiatomic solid-solution nanoparticles produced by chemical or physical fabrication methods, exhibiting significant atomic disorder but with a notable degree of lattice strain due to differences in atomic radii.
generation.intervention: Substitute one or more constituent elements with alternatives having closer atomic radii (and similar catalytic/thermoelectric properties) to reduce the overall lattice strain, while keeping the high-entropy composition intact.
generation.conditions: Expose both the modified and baseline nanoparticles to aging tests and operation conditions at high temperatures (e.g., for catalytic operation at around 900 K in inert or mildly oxidative atmospheres, and for thermoelectric performance tests in the range of 473–1923 K) for extended durations.
generation.structural_mediator: The degree of lattice strain and local atomic ordering modifications induced by reduced atomic size mismatch.
generation.mechanism: Reducing lattice strain decreases the activation energy for atomic diffusion at high temperatures, thereby limiting diffusion-driven elemental segregation and surface oxidation. This preservation of the disordered solid-solution state maintains structural integrity and chemical uniformity under service conditions.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the baseline nanoparticles with larger atomic radius mismatches, the strain-modified nanoparticles will exhibit a slower rate of phase segregation and surface oxidation, leading to improved structural and chemical stability. Functionally, this should translate into better retention of catalytic activity or thermoelectric efficiency over time.
generation.baseline: Nanoparticles synthesized with the full complement of elements having larger atomic radius mismatches, leading to higher lattice strain and enhanced diffusion rates at elevated temperatures.
generation.boundary: The hypothesis applies within the temperature ranges typical for catalytic (773–1173 K) and thermoelectric (473–1923 K) operation. It assumes that the only major difference between intervention and baseline materials is the level of lattice strain due to atomic radius differences, and that other factors (such as overall composition and synthesis method) are held constant.
generation.uncertainty: Precise quantitative thresholds for atomic radius mismatch that distinctly affect diffusion rates and phase stability remain undetermined. Moreover, variations in environmental factors (e.g., partial pressures of reactive gases) could modulate these effects.

falsification_experiment.design: Synthesize two sets of nanoparticles: one set following the baseline composition with larger atomic radius differences, and one set with selected elemental substitutions that minimize atomic size differences. Subject both sets to identical high-temperature aging treatments (e.g., 900 K for 20 hours) in controlled atmospheres (inert or mildly oxidative) and then evaluate phase stability and surface composition.
measurements: X-ray diffraction (XRD) to monitor phase changes and crystallinity
High-resolution transmission electron microscopy (TEM) to observe microstructural evolution
Energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDS) mapping for elemental distribution
Catalytic activity tests or thermoelectric performance measurements pre- and post-aging
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the modified nanoparticles with reduced atomic radius mismatches do not exhibit significantly less phase segregation and surface oxidation compared to the baseline, or if their catalytic/thermoelectric performance does not show superior retention after aging, then the hypothesis is refuted.
